grammarNotes: Tongan is phonetic: words are spelled the way they are pronounced. Stress normally falls on the second-to-last syllable; a toloi (long vowel, e.g. kumā) takes the stress instead.
The fakauʻa (ʻ) is a glottal stop and changes meaning: anga (behavior) vs ʻanga (shark). It is written in front of a vowel or between two vowels.

culture.text: Tongan farewells differ by who is leaving: ʻAlu ā to the person going, Nofo ā to the person staying. Answering both is ʻIo!

quiz.q: Someone is leaving and you are staying. What do you say?
quiz.explain: ʻAlu ā is said to the person who is going; Nofo ā is for the person who stays.

grammarNotes: Each of the five vowels has four forms: plain, with fakauʻa, with toloi, and with both. The fakauʻa is an abrupt glottal stop; the toloi holds the vowel twice as long. Both change word meanings.
No Tongan word ends in a consonant, and two consonants never meet without a vowel between them. ng is one sound, as in English 'singer'.

quiz.explain: The fakauʻa is the glottal stop; the toloi is what lengthens a vowel.
